conceptTag: Apple cuts its product line in 1997
readerTitle: Why Apple got stronger by selling fewer computers
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Apple, 1997~1998 제품 라인 정리) + 일화 (Isaacson 전기 속 회의 장면) + 가상 적용 (식당 메뉴)
insight: 제품 라인의 각 제품이 '누구를 위한 것인지' 한 문장으로 답하지 못하면, 그 제품은 매출을 더하는 게 아니라 고객의 선택과 회사의 집중을 빼앗는다.
misconception: 제품이 많을수록 더 많은 고객을 잡을 수 있고, 어려울 때는 신제품을 더 내는 것이 답이다.

sources.text: Isaacson, W. (2011). Steve Jobs. Simon & Schuster. (복귀 후 제품 회의, 2×2 그리드 일화)
Apple Computer, Form 10-K for fiscal years 1997 and 1998 (1997 적자, 1998 흑자 전환)
Apple press release, February 1998: discontinuation of Newton and eMate
Apple and Microsoft joint announcement, Macworld Boston, August 1997 (Microsoft investment)
Apple press release, May 1998 / August 1998: iMac announcement and shipping

factChecks.note: Jobs의 임시 CEO 취임은 1997년 9월로 널리 알려져 있습니다. 게시 전 Apple 발표 자료로 날짜를 다시 확인하세요.
복귀 당시 Mac 모델 수는 자료마다 다르게 나옵니다. 카드에는 구체적인 숫자 없이 'many overlapping Mac models'로만 적었습니다. '제품의 약 70%를 줄였다'는 흔한 표현도 확인되지 않아 쓰지 않았습니다.
2×2 그리드(consumer/pro × desktop/portable)를 화이트보드에 그렸다는 장면과 '친구에게 어떤 걸 사라고 해야 하나'라는 질문은 Isaacson 전기에 나오는 일화입니다. 카드에 'reportedly'와 일화 표시를 했습니다.
1997 회계연도 대규모 적자(약 10억 달러 규모)와 1998 회계연도 흑자 전환은 10-K로 확인하세요. 카드에는 금액 없이 'heavy losses', 'back to profit'으로만 적었습니다.
Mac 클론 라이선스 종료(1997), Newton 단종 발표(1998년 2월), Microsoft 투자 발표(1997년 8월), iMac 출시(1998년 8월)의 시점을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why Apple got stronger by selling fewer computers
body: In 1997, Apple was in trouble. It was losing heavily, and its shelves were crowded with many overlapping Mac models, plus printers, a handheld called the Newton, and more.
The usual instinct in a crisis is to launch more, so you can reach more customers. Apple did the opposite. It is one of the clearest counterexamples to *more products, more sales*.

image.label: A crowded shelf of nearly identical beige computers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1990년대풍 베이지색 데스크톱 컴퓨터 여러 대가 비슷한 모양으로 빽빽하게 진열된 선반. 각 박스에 헷갈리는 숫자 라벨(예: 'Model 5xxx', 'Model 6xxx'). 실제 Apple 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You just took over. What do you do with the product line?
body: It's late 1997. You run a computer maker that is losing money and market share. Sales staff struggle to explain how one model differs from the next. Your engineers are spread across dozens of projects.

options.text: Keep the line and add one bold new model to win attention
options.feedback: A hit could help, but it lands on a confusing shelf and competes with your own models for engineers and money.

options.text: Cut to a handful of products, each clearly for one kind of customer
options.feedback: You lose some sales and some loyal fans of cut products. In return, customers can choose easily and your best people work on fewer things.

options.text: Quietly drop the worst sellers, about a fifth of the line
options.feedback: It saves some cost with little pain. But the shelf stays confusing, and nobody can say what the company now stands for.

cards.title: Four boxes on a whiteboard.
body: Steve Jobs returned to Apple and became interim CEO in 1997. In his biography, Walter Isaacson tells a story of a product meeting where Jobs reportedly kept asking which models he should tell his friends to buy. Nobody had a clear answer.
He then reportedly drew a **two-by-two grid**: consumer or professional, desktop or portable. Apple would make one great product for each box.
Much of the rest went. Apple ended its licensing of Mac clones, dropped printers, and discontinued the Newton.

image.label: A 2×2 grid: consumer and pro, desktop and portable
image.brief: 화이트보드에 손으로 그린 2×2 그리드. 가로축 'Consumer / Pro', 세로축 'Desktop / Portable'. 네 칸에 각각 단순한 컴퓨터 아이콘 하나씩. 그리드 밖에 X 표시된 작은 제품 아이콘들(프린터, 휴대기기). 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Focus across the whole product line
body: **Product line focus** means every product you sell has one clear job for one clear customer, and no two products do the same job.
Each extra product looks like extra sales. But it also splits customer attention, team effort and the company's story. Focus means saying no to good products, not just bad ones.
The grid worked because a customer could answer one question, *who am I and where do I use it?*, and land on exactly one product.
cards.softwareNote: The same trap shows up as five pricing plans that differ by one feature, or three apps that overlap. If your sales team can't say in one sentence who each plan is for, customers can't either.

cards.title: Fewer products helped in several ways at once.
body: Cutting the line did more than save cost.
list: **Customers:** an easier choice, with no guessing between near-twins
**Engineers:** effort pooled into four products instead of scattered
**Operations:** fewer parts and less inventory to manage
cards.callout: The iMac arrived in 1998 to fill the consumer desktop box, and Apple returned to profit that fiscal year.

cards.title: Cutting alone did not save Apple.
body: The turnaround had many causes: a Microsoft investment announced in 1997, the iMac's design, and tighter operations. Copying the cuts without a strong product to put in each box would just make a smaller, weaker company.
Focus also has real costs. People lost jobs, Newton users lost a product they loved, and clone makers lost a business. Cut only when you know what the remaining products are for.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant with 80 dishes.
body: Your family restaurant's menu has grown to 80 dishes over the years. Guests take a long time to order, the kitchen wastes ingredients, and reviews call the food "fine." Sales are slipping.

options.text: Cut the 30 dishes that sell least, keep the rest as is
options.feedback: Waste drops quickly. But low sales don't tell you which dishes define you, and 50 dishes may still feel like no clear identity.

options.text: Decide who you serve and when, then keep only the dishes that are best for each
options.feedback: Like the grid, each dish earns its place by serving a clear guest and moment. You'll upset some regulars, so tell them why and keep a favorite or two.

options.text: Add a trendy new section to bring in younger guests
options.feedback: It might draw attention, but it makes a long menu longer and stretches a kitchen that is already struggling.

cards.title: Every product should have a box only it can fill.
body: A crowded line feels safe, but it can confuse customers and scatter your team. Apple grew again by making fewer things, each with a clear reason to exist.
**Try it today:** list everything you sell. Next to each item, write who it's for in one sentence. Circle any two that share a sentence.
